extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court justices and clerks; appellate/patent litigators and judges; patent practitioners interested in appellate practice and §101 doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: A petition to the U.S. Supreme Court challenging the Federal Circuit’s frequent use of Rule 36 one-word affirmances and arguing that the practice undermines development of patent law, denies meaningful appellate review, and warrants certiorari; includes appended lower-court opinions illustrating the issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 undermines consistency in patent law
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 36 one-word affirmances provide no reasons for decisions, which impedes clarification of patent law and undermines consistency in patent jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Rule 36 gives no rationale, the Supreme Court (or other reviewing courts) must identify the basis for the decision before deciding whether to grant certiorari—practically insulating such decisions from meaningful review. Example citations/authority: Taylor v. McKeithen, 407 U.S. 191, 194 (1972) (granting relief where record lacked Court of Appeals' insight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate opinions must provide rationale and factual findings for meaningful review
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellate disposition that issues no rationale, findings of fact, conclusions of law, analysis, or explanation denies the public and higher courts the ability to understand the basis for the decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of explanation prevents determining which issues were decided or foreclosed, creating uncertainty for parties and lower courts. Cases cited: Rates Tech., Inc. v. Mediatrix Telecom, Inc., 688 F.3d 742, 750 (Fed. Cir. 2012) (no opinion simply confirms trial court judgment but does not endorse or reject reasoning); TecSec, Inc. v. IBM Corp., 731 F.3d 1336 (Fed. Cir. 2013) (demonstrating reasonable dispute among judges as to grounds when no opinion is given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 one-word decisions erode transparency and public confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently offering no justification for decisions erodes public confidence that each decision rests on principled reasoning and undermines legitimacy of the appellate judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one-word affirmation requires the public to 'simply trust' there is a principled justification; repeated unexplained affirmances reduce confidence in reasoned rule-of-law governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 can insulate errors and encourage lower-court error replication
rubrics_metrics.description: A one-word affirmance can place the Federal Circuit's imprimatur on lower-court decisions that may contain multiple errors, thereby encouraging lower courts to emulate those erroneous dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating a Rule 36 affirmance as a signal that the lower-court decision is 'good law' even where the disposition may have substantive or procedural errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 may raise due process and equal protection concerns when it prevents meaningful appellate review
rubrics_metrics.description: Denying reasoned appellate review through unexplained affirmances risks infringing constitutional rights to due process and equal protection by preventing review based on a reliable, credible record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative support: U.S. Const. amend. XIV, § 1; Townes v. Alabama, 586 U.S. 977, 980 (2018) (reliability of record essential for review); Parker v. Dugger, 498 U.S. 308, 321 (1991) (meaningful appellate review requires consideration of the actual record).

rubrics_metrics.name: Where an appeals court applies a regular rule affecting all patent litigation, the issue is of special national importance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Federal Circuit consistently applies a practice (e.g., vacating declaratory judgments for mootness or routine Rule 36 affirmances), that practice may be a matter of special importance warranting Supreme Court review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cardinal Chemical Co. v. Morton Int'l, 508 U.S. 83, 89 (1993) — Supreme Court granted certiorari because the Federal Circuit’s practice was regularly applied and had nationwide effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Circuit must comply with statutory requirement to issue mandate and opinion from PTAB decisions (35 U.S.C. § 144)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of unexplained one-word affirmances can conflict with statutory requirements that the Federal Circuit issue a mandate and opinion from Patent Trial and Appeal Board decisions under 35 U.S.C. § 144.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule 36 creates tension with statutory expectations for reasoned appellate dispositions in certain contexts involving the PTO/PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 36 decisions make it unknowable which ground the appellate court relied upon when multiple grounds exist
rubrics_metrics.description: When a lower disposition was decided on alternative grounds, a Rule 36 affirmation leaves parties and the public unable to determine which justification the court relied on, producing reasonable dispute even among Federal Circuit judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case example: TecSec, Inc. v. IBM Corp., 731 F.3d 1336, 1350–51 (Fed. Cir. 2013) (Reyna, J., dissenting as to whether disposition was based on alternative grounds). Practical effect: prevents clarity on precedential reach and foreclosed issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: RCFC 59(e) extraordinary-circumstances standard for motions to alter or amend judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion to alter or amend judgment under RCFC 59(e) will be granted only in 'extraordinary circumstances,' including (1) an intervening change in controlling law, (2) availability of new evidence, or (3) the need to correct clear error or prevent manifest injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: IAP Worldwide Servs., Inc. v. United States, 141 Fed. Cl. 788, 801 (2019); Johnson v. United States, 127 Fed. Cl. 661, 663 (2016). Motions that merely rehash previously rejected arguments are improper; reconsideration is not a vehicle for relitigation. See Froudi v. United States, 22 Cl. Ct. 290, 300 (1991).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 15(a)(2) — leave to amend pleadings should be 'freely given' absent reasons to deny
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave to amend should be freely given when justice requires unless an apparent or declared reason exists to refuse (e.g., futility, undue delay, bad faith, repeated failure to cure deficiencies, or undue prejudice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court authority: Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178, 182 (1962). Practical application in post-judgment context: the court evaluates whether amendment is futile or whether the plaintiff repeatedly failed to cure deficiencies in prior amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foman futility standard and denial of leave to amend
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment may be denied if it would be futile — for example, it would do no more than state an alternative theory for recovery or the plaintiff has repeatedly failed to cure deficiencies by prior amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may deny leave where prior amendments failed to address deficiencies and where the court’s prior analysis shows underlying legal defects (cited: Foman). Example from the opinion: plaintiff amended twice and a third amendment would be futile given the court’s detailed §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 (Alice/Mayo two-step framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate (1) whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea), and if so (2) whether the claim elements, individually or as an ordered combination, amount to 'significantly more' — an inventive concept that transforms the abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical application: courts may treat claims directed to 'collecting, analyzing, manipulating, and displaying data' or 'filtering patient [physical] signals to increase accuracy' as abstract ideas; to survive, a pleading must allege specific, plausible factual allegations showing the claim amounts to significantly more than the abstract idea (citing Alice; Aatrix Software, Inc. v. Green Shades Software, Inc., 882 F.3d 1121 (Fed. Cir. 2018)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings standard for §101 challenges (sufficiency of allegations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a motion to dismiss under RCFC 12(b)(6), a plaintiff must plead specific, plausible factual allegations sufficient to show that the patent in practice amounts to 'significantly more' than an abstract idea and/or that its techniques were implemented in a specific combination or in an uncommon manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the complaint fails to recite such specific factual allegations, dismissal for failure to state a claim is appropriate. The court in this case held plaintiff did not plead facts demonstrating an inventive concept and therefore the patents were directed to ineligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to vacate or amend judgment are not vehicles for relitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions under reconsideration procedures (e.g., RCFC 59(e)) that merely reassert arguments already presented and rejected are improper; they must present extraordinary circumstances to justify relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court quoted that reconsideration 'is not a vehicle for giving an unhappy litigant an additional chance to sway the judge' (Froudi). Arguments more appropriately belong on appeal rather than a motion for reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: When evaluating patent claims, courts consider the patents 'as a whole' and may dismiss claims directed to abstract ideas even where the specification describes advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts look to the character of the claimed invention as a whole. Even if the specification describes purposes like facilitating diagnosis or eliminating background noise, the claims may still be directed to an abstract idea absent an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from opinion: despite descriptions of a 'simple interface' or noise-reduction objectives in the specification, the court found the claims directed to abstract ideas (collecting/processing/displaying data) and lacking the required inventive concept; thus, factual allegations about purported improvements must connect to claim elements that amount to 'significantly more.'
